hints: Look closely at what methotrexate stops: nucleotides containing thymine. Where in the cell is thymine used in large amounts?
The cell is already entering telophase when treated, so it will finish this mitosis. In which upcoming stage must new DNA be made by copying all the chromosomes?
walkthrough:
**Work out what the drug really stops**

Think simple. Thymine is a base found only in DNA, not in RNA or protein.

If you cannot make thymine nucleotides, you cannot make new DNA:
$$no\ thymine\ nucleotides = no\ DNA\ synthesis$$

**Recall when DNA is made in the cell cycle**

DNA is not made during mitosis. It is copied during the S phase, which is part of interphase.

Interphase is the long growth phase between divisions when chromosomes are replicated before the next mitosis.

**Apply the timing to this cell**

This cell is already entering telophase, the last stage of mitosis. Its chromosomes have already been copied and separated.

So it will finish telophase and divide, then enter the next interphase. That is when it tries to replicate DNA, fails because of methotrexate, and cannot complete the cell cycle.

options.A: Anaphase separates already copied chromatids. No new DNA synthesis happens here, so lack of thymine nucleotides has no effect.
options.B: Interphase includes S phase where DNA replication occurs. Without thymine nucleotides the cell cannot copy its DNA and cannot continue the cycle.
options.C: Metaphase lines up already replicated chromosomes on the spindle. It does not require new nucleotide synthesis.
options.D: Prophase condenses chromosomes that were already replicated in the previous interphase. It does not need new thymine nucleotides.
